entries.before:
The scan experiments reveal two execution regimes. With one block per
query, batch 8 exposes only eight blocks on a 170-SM device. Candidate
partitioning increases the available block parallelism. In the independent-bound grouped-scan
experiment, eight groups improve end-to-end throughput by
$2.06$--$2.76\times$ at batch 8. Profiling supports a stage-level
explanation: arXiv's scan falls from about 849 to 216\,$\mu$s, Vogue's
from 1,059 to 246\,$\mu$s, and OpenAI-3072's from 728 to 155\,$\mu$s.
The additional merges cost approximately 16.7, 9.1 and 3.7\,$\mu$s,
respectively. The net reduction is large even after paying for merging.

At batch 1,000 there are already enough independent queries to expose
many blocks. Additional groups repeat table staging, local-buffer
admission and sorting, and produce extra merge traffic. The independent-bound
grouped path can fall to about $0.46\times$ its one-block baseline on
arXiv at $\alpha=200$. The full-batch profiles show scan increasing from
2,922 to 6,079\,$\mu$s at $\alpha=100$ and from 3,530 to
7,652\,$\mu$s at $\alpha=200$, with an additional 2,624\,$\mu$s
merge in the latter case. This opposing result is central to the design:
parallel decomposition solves insufficient concurrency, but incurs work
that can dominate once concurrency is adequate. Shared bounds reduce
that extra work but do not eliminate the regime change.
entries.after:
For a fixed workload and timing boundary, separate scan, merge and
remaining execution time:
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
 T^{(g)}&=T_{\rm scan}^{(g)}+T_{\rm merge}^{(g)}+T_{\rm other}^{(g)},\\
 \Delta T(g)&=T^{(g)}-T^{(0)},\qquad
 T^{(g)}<T^{(0)}\iff\Delta T(g)<0.
 \end{aligned}
 \label{eq:7-group-cost}
\end{equation}
Here $g=0$ denotes the query-centric implementation and $g>0$ a grouped
path. The three time categories are disjoint: staging and local
selection already included in scan time are not charged again.
This is an accounting identity, not an analytical latency predictor.

At batch 8, one block per query exposes only eight blocks on 170 SMs.
Eight scan groups improve end-to-end throughput by $2.06$--$2.76\times$.
For example, arXiv's scan falls from 849 to 216\,$\mu$s while merging
adds 16.7\,$\mu$s. At batch 1,000, arXiv with $\alpha=200$ instead
increases scan time from 3,530 to 7,652\,$\mu$s and adds
2,624\,$\mu$s of merging; the independent-bound path reaches only
about $0.46\times$ its one-block throughput. Extra parallelism repays
its duplicated work in the first regime and loses in the second.
Shared bounds reduce work without removing this regime change.
entries.reason: Replace repeated regime explanation by a disjoint cost identity plus opposing measured examples

\begin{proof}
A reference item has fewer than $k$ predecessors in the largest survivor
set. If it is present in a smaller set, restriction cannot introduce new
predecessors, so it remains in that set's exact top-$k$. Thus the
intersection with the reference equals the reference items present in
the survivor set. Nestedness can only add such items. Summing missing
reference counts over queries proves the inequality.
\end{proof}
entries.after:
\begin{proof}
For $x\in\mathcal R_{\rm ref}\cap C_\alpha$, the common total order gives
\begin{equation*}
 |\{y\in C_\alpha:y\prec x\}|
 \leq|\{y\in C_{\alpha_{\rm ref}}:y\prec x\}|<k.
\end{equation*}
Hence $x\in\mathcal R_\alpha$. Together with
$\mathcal R_\alpha\subseteq C_\alpha$, this proves the intersection
identity in \cref{eq:6-monotonicity}. Nestedness gives
$|C_\alpha\cap\mathcal R_{\rm ref}|
 \leq|C_\beta\cap\mathcal R_{\rm ref}|$.
Summing missing reference counts over queries proves
$D_S(\alpha)\geq D_S(\beta)$.
\end{proof}
entries.reason: Write the predecessor-count implication explicitly; retain the proposition and all its assumptions unchanged

The implementation uses CUDA's SIMT execution: threads are organised into
blocks and 32-thread warps, with registers, block-shared memory and device
global memory serving different reuse scopes \cite{cuda_programming_guide}.
Coalescing groups neighbouring lane accesses into suitable memory
transactions; it does not require fewer logical code bits. Candidate-parallel
primary scanning assigns lanes to neighbouring vectors, while refinement
assigns several lanes to one survivor's coordinates. These mappings exploit
different available parallelism, so one mapping need not suit both stages.

Occupancy is constrained by registers, shared state and block geometry.
More resident threads can hide latency, but more blocks per query can also
duplicate tables and local candidate buffers. Shared memory is valuable
when query data are reused enough to repay loading and synchronisation.
These observations motivate Chapter 5's table grouping, packed access and
batch-aware scheduling; the throughput ablations assess their combined
effects. A claim of bandwidth saturation or a specific cache bottleneck
would additionally require counters and a consistent physical-byte model.

Selection is itself substantial computation. Faiss's GPU work combines
efficient distance processing with warp-oriented selection
\cite{johnson_gpu}. Bitonic networks, radix methods and merge-based
approaches provide established building blocks with different $k$, input
length and state costs. AIR top-$k$ and GridSelect further illustrate why
global selection design depends on workload and whether scores arrive
on the fly \cite{gpu_topk}. This thesis adapts such ideas to JHQ's probe
selection and survivor retention; it does not claim to invent these primitives.

CUDA Graph replay reduces repeated launch setup for a captured workload.
Capture, workspace allocation and changes in graph shape belong to the
index/search lifecycle, rather than the mathematical scoring rule.
Likewise, publishing a shared threshold requires an explicit ordering and
memory-access contract. Correct scalar scores do not alone prove concurrent
admission safe. Chapter 5 separates these correctness conditions from
performance measurements, and Chapter 3 keeps device profiling distinct
from the host-visible search interval.

Graph ANN replaces list scanning with navigation through promising
neighbourhoods. Its benefit is to avoid scoring most database vectors;
its GPU difficulty is the dependency between discovering a neighbour and
deciding which neighbourhood to expand. SONG separates graph search into
stages to expose distance parallelism and controls dynamic memory overhead
\cite{song}. This is an alternative access strategy, rather than a different
implementation of JHQ's fixed routed candidate universe.

CAGRA designs graph construction and search for GPU parallelism, including
small- and large-batch queries \cite{cagra}. Its graph connectivity and
search width expose a different tuning surface from IVF probes. Storing
edges and vectors creates a capacity trade-off; quantised-vector CAGRA is
also relevant, so fp32 CAGRA alone is an incomplete compressed-index
comparison. The thesis measures both in E1. Their different operating
regions are reported under the common boundary rather than inferred from
cross-paper speedup numbers.

BANG targets a different capacity regime: it keeps compressed vectors on
the GPU and accesses the host-resident graph through CPU/GPU cooperation
\cite{bang}. Capacity is obtained by distributing the working structures,
with transfer and coordination becoming part of the design. Its billion-scale
results demonstrate an alternative to complete device residency, not
capacity evidence for this thesis. The present JHQ implementation retains
its compressed search index on one device and has no comparable host-graph
execution path.

The comparison therefore turns on access regularity, representation and
residency, not a general graph-versus-quantisation hierarchy. Graph navigation
can be attractive for a small number of queries; list scans expose regular
code access and abundant batch work. Either can be bottlenecked by selection
or movement. Which wins at a target recall is an empirical question for a
specified device, memory budget and workload. E1 tests that question at batch
1,000; internal small-batch JHQ gains do not answer it for graph competitors.

\subsection{Learning a representation versus exploiting its structure}

Optimised product quantisation learns the space decomposition and codebooks
to reduce quantisation distortion \cite{opq}. Its rotation is optimised for
the data, whereas JHQ's random square rotation supports a cheap analytical
primary model. The trade-off involves fitting cost, reconstruction fidelity
and scorer structure. Improving a general learned codebook does not
automatically preserve the internal Cartesian product needed by an exact
16+16 decomposition.

ScaNN's anisotropic quantisation work instead weights error according to
its relevance to maximum-inner-product retrieval, showing why reconstruction
MSE is not the only useful objective \cite{scann}. Its objective and
implementation setting differ from the squared-L2 hierarchical pipeline
here. The useful comparison is the choice of loss: a rank-sensitive
representation should be tested against actual retained-neighbour quality
and execution cost. The stopped rank-oriented experiment in Chapter 8
provides an example of this distinction within JHQ.

\subsection{Small lookup tables have substantial prior art}

PQ Fast Scan replaces reliance on cache-resident tables with tables suited
to CPU SIMD registers \cite{fastscan}. Quicker ADC generalises register
lookup techniques and introduces irregular quantisers and split tables
\cite{quickeradc}. These works establish that table shape and the execution
instruction set must be designed together. This thesis's claim is the exact
decomposition available from its inherited Cartesian coordinate structure,
and its measured implementation on a GPU. CPU SIMD results are conceptual
precedents, not throughput measurements on the tested GPU. FP32 table
association and cutoff ties still require separate numerical checking.

RaBitQ also uses randomised quantisation and compact sign information,
with a distance estimator and theoretical error analysis
\cite{rabitq}. Multi-bit extensions trade storage for estimator accuracy
\cite{rabitq_multi}. Their guarantees attach to their specified constructions
and estimator assumptions. They cannot be transferred to JHQ merely because
both use rotations and binary components. In JHQ, primary signs select
survivors and an explicitly stored residual supplies the next precision
level; the resulting quality depends on both truncation and reconstruction.

GPU IVF-RaBitQ brings this family into a complete GPU build/search design,
including GPU-oriented distance computation and fused search
\cite{ivfrabitq}. It is therefore a particularly relevant contemporary
baseline, rather than background evidence of a missing GPU quantiser.
Its fused execution makes clear that compact codes alone are insufficient:
the access and selection pipeline must also be competitive. E1 includes
multiple bit budgets, and its high-recall results limit any broad claim
of JHQ dominance.

\subsection{Refinement effort and adaptive stopping}

Candidate expansion and reranking already appear in Faiss's
\texttt{k\_factor} and cuVS refinement controls
\cite{faiss_refine,cuvs_refinement}. Faiss autotuning can use GT-labelled
queries to search recall--time trade-offs \cite{faiss_autotune}. Learned
adaptive termination predicts sufficient search effort
\cite{li_termination}; DARTH frames early termination around declarative
recall targets \cite{darth}. These are relevant alternatives to spending a
uniform effort everywhere. Chapter 6's particular policy selects one
workload-level survivor multiplier using unlabelled agreement with a larger
budget. It avoids a trained predictor, while inheriting the reference's
quality limits. This distinction is the policy's scope, rather than a claim
that adaptive search or refinement budgets are new ideas.
